## General
# Principles of Practical Wisdom.
---

### 1.
Before all else, young man! when you first step out into the world, take note of the following principles, which are taught not by abstract classroom study <term>Katheders-studium: formal university lectures delivered from a professor's chair</term>, nor by "closet philosophy" <note>The original *Stubenphilosophie* refers to academic theories developed in isolation, lacking real-world application.</note>—but by experience.

Accustom your mind to teachability and attentiveness; without these, everything evaporates, and you will retain nothing for yourself. It will happen to you as it does to an unskilled chemist <note>original: *Chymiker*</note>, who does not seal his vessels properly and therefore keeps nothing.

### 2.
Consider that nothing is necessary to you but your duty; nothing estimable but virtue. Both of these relate to all your actions. What these [demand] of

you demand; arrange your whole life accordingly.

->3.<-

Honor is, to be sure, only a human creation <note>original: *Menschenwerk*</note> in respect to temporal matters—in itself nothing—but through the length of time that it has been accepted among people, it has gained so much prestige and weight that it must be more precious to a person than other temporal goods. One cannot, therefore, watch over one’s good reputation <note>original: *Ruf*</note> carefully enough; one cannot be cautious enough in preserving an earned good name.

->4.<sup>b</sup><-

Young people commonly possess a great volatility of spirit <note>original: *Flüchtigkeit des Geistes*</note>, which easily lapses into recklessness if one is not well on one's guard. Strive to fix the instability of your mind and to tame your wild imagination. Do not hurry without necessity, and seek to guide your liveliness into a moderate pace, to lead it onto the path of dispassionate judgment <term>kaltblütigen Beurtheilung: literally "cold-blooded" judgment, referring to the ability to make calm, objective decisions unaffected by heat of passion or youthful impulse</term> when you feel yourself being carried away by it.

<meta>This page continues the series of numbered moral aphorisms, specifically focusing on the internal motivations for virtue and the balance between greed and extravagance. It follows the previous page's discussion on social conduct and intellectual depth.</meta>

<image-desc>A small horizontal decorative ornament consisting of abstract floral and scroll patterns.</image-desc>

### 13.

Do not insist too much on obtaining a superficial respect from others; do not beg for their approval. In your actions, seek no other glory than that of having performed them; do good for the sake of goodness itself. This is the true foundation upon which you should build your reputation <note>original: *Namen*; literally "name," referring to one's character or standing in the community.</note>, and in this way, you will compel people to have genuine respect for you.

### 14.

Flee from greed; among all vices, it is the lowest. The spendthrift makes himself contemptible; the miser is universally hated. Excessive frugality <note>original: *Häuslichkeit*; while often meaning "domesticity," here it refers to an obsessive concern with household economy that leads to stinginess.</note> will find it difficult to remain within the boundaries of virtue. Be magnanimous and generous; imagine that you lose whatever you do not give away; but to avoid becoming a spendthrift, always seek counsel from prudence; without her, there is no virtue.

### 15.

Do not count on human gratitude when you wish to do good; do not worry that you might create ungrateful people through your kindness; do good without any selfish intent. Kind deeds are never lost; even ingratitude makes them known <note>The author suggests that even when a recipient is ungrateful, the act of kindness is still a public testament to the giver's character.</note>.

If you are able to perform a service for someone, always combine it with kindness and goodwill; the manner in which you place someone under an obligation doubles the value of that obligation. Do not wait until your friend is in need of your assistance; always anticipate his needs to the best of your ability. By doing so, you will spare him a painful step that humbles human <term>self-love (Eigenliebe)<gloss>In this context, a person's sense of dignity or pride.</gloss></term>—the act of having to appeal to your emotions on behalf of his difficult circumstances. You will show him that true friendship is helpful without needing to be asked.

<vocab>Gratitude, Kind Deeds, Ingratitude, Service, Courtesy, Obligation, Assistance, Self-love, Friendship</vocab>

<summary>This page offers moral advice on the nature of altruism and friendship, emphasizing that good deeds should be done without expectation of reward and that true friends anticipate each other's needs to preserve their dignity.</summary>
<keywords>ethics, friendship, gratitude, altruism, self-love, social obligations, kindness</keywords>

### 22.

I want to tell you a great **secret** so that you will be well-liked in the world: Always think, speak, and act in the way that is most appropriate for the moment.

This is a **principle of politeness** <note>The German word "Höflichkeit" here implies not just manners, but the art of "courtliness" or social grace required to navigate various social circles successfully.</note> that you can never make your own enough, because you need it everywhere, and without it you will rarely achieve anything.

### 23.

To spare yourself **regret**, do not be too hasty in your decisions, and reflect long upon the matter you undertake.

### 24.

It will be difficult, given the youthful **vivacity** <note>original: "Lebhaftigkeit"</note> of your spirit, to let the stream of your words flow freely without weakening their **sense**. <term>Sense<gloss>The original "Verstand" can mean intellect, reason, or the logical coherence of one's speech.</gloss></term>

Accustom yourself to a **composed manner of speaking**, and before you speak, reflect well upon what you wish to say.

->25.<-

The life of a young person should resemble a **public speech**, where all its parts are correctly connected with one another, and all aim toward a single purpose; it is exactly the same with the **actions** of a human being.

### 28.

Take careful heed that you make no enemies; there is no one who cannot do you harm.

Nothing is more hateful than hatred itself; it is a domestic enemy <note>The original term "Hausfeind" refers to an enemy within one's own house or, metaphorically, a private vice or internal struggle that one cannot escape.</note> that one carries around everywhere.

If one gives ear to its hostile voice, one plunges into an abyss of more evils than one has wished upon others out of hatred.

Insults harm only those who inflict them upon others.

The secret to ensuring they do not cause you vexation consists in forgetting them, provided they do not attack your honor.

This is called punishing oneself for the faults of others, when one feels anger toward those who wish to provoke us.

### 38.

Never judge or pass sentence based on appearance, which can be deceptive.

Be lenient toward the faults of your neighbor <note>original: "Nächsten." In this 18th-century context, this refers generally to other people or fellow human beings, echoing the biblical command to love one's neighbor.</note>, if you wish for your own to be excused as well.

### 39.

All people are born for society. Those who contribute most to the pleasantness of it should also be the most sought after.

The science of the world <note>original: "Die Wissenschaft der Welt." This refers to social intelligence or the art of living ("savoir-vivre"), rather than academic study.</note> consists in the art of pleasing. Therefore, do not insist so much on erudition <term>erudition: extensive knowledge acquired from books; deep, formal learning</term> as on combining the pleasant and agreeable aspects of your nature with it.

Scholars by profession are usually unrefined, ill-mannered people. They have so much to do with the dead <note>Referring to their study of ancient texts, history, and deceased authors.</note> that they do not know how to live with the living.

### 40.

Learn to set limits for yourself in all your duties through the rules of reason <note>original: "Vernunft." In the Enlightenment context, this refers to the capacity for rational thought and moral judgment that distinguishes humans from animals.</note>.

### 41.

### 43.

### 44.

Think: nothing is good, nothing beautiful but truth; it reveals itself in the heart and allows its pleasantness to be tasted.

### 87.

Memory loses its strength when it lacks subject matter and nourishment; tend to your own if you wish to preserve it well.

Memory is the treasure-house of the understanding <note>original: "Verstand" — the faculty of reason or intellect</note>; the storehouse from which the mind <note>original: "Geist" — can mean spirit or intellect</note> draws its provisions; however, the power of judgment <note>original: "Beurtheilungskraft"</note> must first apply them correctly and give them value.

## Reverence for the Authors of our Existence.
<note>The "Authors of our existence" (Urheber unsers Daseyns) is a formal, Enlightenment-era phrasing for one's parents.</note>

It is not merely a principle of <term>prudence<note>original: "Klugheit" — in this context, it refers to practical wisdom or self-interested common sense.</note></term>—no, it is an inviolable law—a law that from time immemorial has been observed by the <term>most primitive peoples<note>original: "rohesten Völker" — literally "rawest," referring to societies the author considers to be in a state of nature.</note></term> just as much as by the most <term>civilized<note>original: "policirtesten" — referring to societies with refined laws, governance, and manners.</note></term>.

This is proof that this law, which the Creator carved into our hearts, already resides within nature itself.

The voice of nature is often too weak to reach the ears of reason amidst the <term>turmoil of the passions<note>original: "Aufruhr der Leidenschaften" — a common philosophical theme of the era, suggesting that intense emotions can drown out one's moral compass.</note></term>; and therefore it is also a divine law that threatens the transgressor with the strictest <term>retribution<note>original: "Ahndung" — a formal term for punishment or divine justice.</note></term>.

## Reverence for the Authors of our Existence.

It is not merely a principle of <term>prudence<note>original: "Klugheit" — in the 18th century, this often referred to "worldly wisdom" or acting out of practical self-interest rather than pure moral conviction.</note></term> — no, it is an inviolable law — a law that from time immemorial the most primitive peoples, as well as the most <term>civilized<note>original: "policirtesten" — from the French "policé," meaning societies characterized by refined laws, education, and social order.</note></term>, have observed.

This is proof that this law, which the Creator engraved into our hearts, already lies within nature itself.

The voice of nature is often too weak to reach the ears of reason amidst the turmoil of the passions; and for that reason, it is also a divine law that threatens the <term>transgressor<note>original: "Uibertretter" (modern: Übertreter) — one who steps over or violates a moral or legal boundary.</note></term> with the most severe retribution.

## The Importance of Education.

---

It is certainly true that children are punishable when they withhold the obedience and proper reverence they owe to their parents; however, the crime of parents who neglect the <term>education<note>original: "Erziehung" — In this 18th-century context, this term encompasses more than schooling; it refers to the total moral, social, and spiritual "upbringing" or "rearing" of a child.</note></term> of their children is no less significant: for the <term>well-being and woe<note>original: "Wohl und Weh" — an idiomatic expression meaning the total welfare or "for better or worse" of one's life circumstances.</note></term> of our lives depends almost entirely on the upbringing we receive.

He who is born with a natural inclination toward evil becomes an inexhaustible source of all <term>vices<note>original: "Laster" — immoral habits or character flaws, often viewed in this period as the direct opposite of virtues.</note></term> unless a careful education improves him early on and steers his heart toward the good.

But even a heart with the finest <term>disposition<note>original: "Anlage" — refers to the natural talents, potential, or temperament a person is born with.</note></term> is corrupted if it is left to itself without care.

<vocab>Education, Children, Parents, Obedience, Reverence, Crime, Well-being and woe, Vice, Heart</vocab>

<summary>This page argues that while children owe obedience to their parents, parents commit an equally great crime if they neglect their children's moral upbringing. It emphasizes that education is the only force capable of correcting natural flaws and preserving natural goodness.</summary>
<keywords>education, parenting, moral responsibility, vice, disposition, character formation</keywords>

The education of one's child should begin by studying their <term>inclinations<note>original: "Hang" — in 18th-century pedagogy, this refers to a child's natural leaning or innate tendency toward certain behaviors.</note></term>, their taste, and their passions; their inclinations in order to guide them; their passions in order to moderate them; their taste in order to elevate it; their faults in order to improve them; their good qualities in order to make them dear to the child, and their failings in order to make the child mindful of them. One must therefore either give up entirely on a good upbringing for one's children, or keep them constantly under one's eyes and do everything possible to become their friend.

## Academic Disciplines.
---

Under this heading, I include everything a young person ought to learn, according to the <term>vocation<note>original: "Berufe" — in the 18th century, this carried the weight of a "calling" or a specific station in life for which one was destined.</note></term> for which they are intended; what the ultimate goal of their studies should be; and finally, the proper use they should make of their knowledge.

Not everyone can learn everything; each person must primarily choose those subjects through which they wish to <term>earn their bread<note>original: "sein Brod gewinnen" — a common idiom for securing a livelihood or financial independence.</note></term> and be of service to the whole of society. It would, therefore, be extremely unwise to devote oneself to disciplines or arts that either do not harmonize with one's primary field of study or that hinder one's progress toward <term>mastery<note>original: "Vollkommenheit" — literally "perfection," referring to the highest level of professional or academic achievement.</note></term> in that field.

<vocab>Academic Disciplines, Vocations, Studies, Earning a Living, Mastery</vocab>

All our knowledge is contemptible if it does not have the welfare of our <term>fellow human beings<note>original: "Nebenmenschen" — literally "those who stand beside us," referring to our neighbors or society at large.</note></term> as its purpose alongside our own. Benefiting the world through significant discoveries, through kind instruction, and through the spread of useful knowledge is the noble ultimate goal of all <term>sciences<note>original: "Wissenschaften" — in the 18th century, this term encompassed all formal academic disciplines and scholarship, not just the natural sciences.</note></term>, without which they are dead and, in the eyes of the wise, without value.

The use of this knowledge must be no less noble and useful; otherwise, the sciences are a gleaming dagger in the hand of a madman; a burning torch in the hand of the <term>Herostratus<note>Herostratus was an arsonist who destroyed the Temple of Artemis in 356 BCE solely to ensure his name would be remembered; the author uses him here as a symbol of someone who uses power or knowledge for destructive infamy.</note></term> of humanity.

In every science lie hidden several truths; since it is the natural desire of man himself to come to know the truth, one will always devote oneself to the sciences with pleasure.

## On the Obedience Owed to the Laws of a State.

---

The maintenance of <term>civil society<note>original: "bürgerliche Gesellschaft" — in the context of Enlightenment political philosophy, this refers to a community of people living under a unified system of law and government, rather than in a "state of nature."</note></term> and the general welfare of nations demand from every member of the state that he submits himself to its laws.

In a monarchical state, the subject is duty-bound to render his reverence and obedience to the King; in a republican state, one is duty-bound to obey the <term>magistrates<note>original: "Vorsteher" — literally "those who stand before"; this refers to elected officials, leaders, or superiors who head a republic.</note></term>.

This law admits no exception; it is [essential] for the preservation of the welfare of all—

# On the Submission Owed to the Laws of a State.

---

The maintenance of <term>civil society<note>original: "bürgerliche Gesellschaft" — in Enlightenment political theory, this refers to a community of citizens living under a unified system of law and government rather than in a "state of nature."</note></term> and the general welfare of nations demand from every member of the state that they submit to its laws.

In a monarchical state, the <term>subject<note>original: "Unterthan" — an individual who lives under the rule of a sovereign and owes them allegiance.</note></term> is duty-bound to show reverence and obedience to the King; in a republican state, one is duty-bound to obey the <term>leaders<note>original: "Vorstehern" — the elected or appointed magistrates and officials who head a republic.</note></term>.

Anything that has been maintained in a state through long habit should only be changed when there are stronger reasons for the <term>abolition<note>original: "Aufhebung" — the formal repeal or ending of a law, custom, or institution.</note></term> of the matter than those by which it was originally introduced: specifically, when the abolition is more beneficial to the general good of society than its preservation; and in such a case, every member is obligated to contribute their part.

Innovations, which many dissatisfied people have wished to introduce into the <term>constitution<note>original: "Verfassung" — here referring to the established legal and political structure of a realm rather than a single written document.</note></term> of a realm, would often serve more toward the downfall of the state than toward the securing of its <term>prosperity<note>original: "Glückseligkeit" — a key Enlightenment term meaning the collective happiness, well-being, and flourishing of a people.</note></term>; the state would sooner lose its power than increase it. The truth of this statement is confirmed by a thousand cases in history.

The complaint of rebels regarding the cruelty and oppression of their <term>sovereigns<note>original: "Oberherren" — the high authorities, lords, or rulers who hold power over a territory.</note></term> will never serve as an excuse <note>The author suggests that perceived tyranny does not justify the chaos of rebellion.</note>.

## Against the Instigators of Public Unrest and Conspiracies.

---

**F**rom the principles already established, it is easy to conclude how criminal those are who—under the pretext of bringing about the abolition of certain abuses—incite unrest in the state. ## Birth and Rank.

It would be better for a man of rank <term>Stand: social status or position within a tiered class hierarchy</term> to lose his life than to lose his honor through a crime or a shameful action.

The higher he is by birth, the more contemptible <note>original: "verächtlicher"</note> he also becomes if he deviates from the virtue of his ancestors <term>Vorältern: forefathers or previous generations whose reputation the current heir must uphold</term>.

Wealth, positions of honor, and a high birth elevate the merit of those who have already earned general respect; however, these very same advantages are also what increase the humiliation and the shame of those who, through their excesses <note>original: "Ausschweifungen"; referring to debauchery, profligacy, or lack of self-control</note>—

## On the Choice of One's Profession.

---

Haste in the choice of one's station <note>original: "Standes"—this term refers to one's social rank, vocation, or professional "estate" in life</note> can have dangerous consequences for a person.

One should not decide upon it until one has accurately come to know one's inclinations, one's strengths, and one's talents: Then, one must also consider whether one is capable of fulfilling the duties associated with the chosen profession; whether one feels strong enough to endure the labors and hardships that occur within it.

<keywords>self-interest, social exclusion, career choice, vocational discernment, duty, self-knowledge, perseverance</keywords>

In this situation, one should seek advice from a friend who knows the world and thinks wisely and clearly. To this person, one should frankly open the most secret folds of one's heart; reveal to him one's passions, inclinations, and one's entire way of thinking.

It is immediately necessary to place distrust in oneself and to observe oneself most strictly.

Our heart has too many weaknesses by which self-love <note>original: "Eigenliebe"—in this period, this term often carried a negative connotation of vanity or narcissism rather than healthy self-esteem</note> masters it; hence there is so much self-deception in the choice of one's station <note>original: "Standes"—referring to one's social and professional rank</note>; one believes oneself fit for every profession that flatters our self-love, where the passions see a free field.

Self-love should therefore never have a part in a decision that must be made at one of the most important moments of life.

A miser <note>original: "Geitziger"</note>, a drunkard, a libertine <note>original: "Wohllüstling"; one who pursues physical pleasure without moral restraint</note>, a gambler are never fit to be true friends; vice does not unite with virtue, and a union of vice with vice can never be called friendship.

Least of all should you form a friendship with sentimentalists <note>original: "Empfindlern"; referring to the 18th-century "Empfindsamkeit" or Sentimentalism movement which emphasized exaggerated, often performative emotion</note>; they sigh and whine into your ears with tender elegies; yet in reality, they are as hollow as the sounds they utter.

The most dangerous reef upon which all friendship founders is self-interest <note>original: "Interesse"; here specifically meaning financial or personal gain</note>. Try to protect your friend's interests as much as possible, and do not make a friendship with anyone whose character is primarily marked by selfishness; you are merely the source from which he wishes to draw for himself; and then he values you only so long as he finds something in you; and if this is gone, he will never want to be your friend.

# Obligations Toward a Friend.

---

There is no such thing as a perfect human being; one must therefore indulgently <note>original: "nachsichtig"; meaning with forbearance or leniency</note> endure the faults of one's friends, or else renounce all friendship entirely.

But must one also be at the service of those one loves in every circumstance? — This question is easily answered, as I have already mentioned it above when the choice of a friend <note>Referring to the discussion on pages 163-164 regarding the moral character required for a lasting bond</note> was discussed.

## One must have various kinds of friends.

---

Among all the principles of a true doctrine of prudence <note>original: "Klugheitslehre"; a genre of 18th-century literature providing practical advice on social success and moral conduct</note>, this one is certainly not among the least important:

Whoever lives at court or within the circle of high society <note>original: "grossen Welt"; literally the "great world," referring to the elite social and political spheres</note> requires a thousand different forms of support: sometimes a friend’s counsel to be able to behave wisely; a beneficial admonition to abandon this or that fault; financial support to be able to cover the most necessary expenses during many a moment of embarrassment; or the affection of a great personage <note>original: "eines Grossen"; a high-ranking noble or powerful official</note> in order to advance in rank or to maintain the position one already holds.

## One Must Have Different Kinds of
## Friends.

---

Among all the principles of a true doctrine of prudence <term>Klugheitslehre: the 18th-century study of practical wisdom, social savvy, and the "art of living" successfully in society</term>, this one is certainly not one of the least important:

Whoever lives at court or in the circles of the "great world" <note>original: "grossen Welt"; a contemporary term for the aristocratic and fashionable social scene.</note> requires a thousand kinds of support: sometimes a friend’s counsel, in order to be able to conduct oneself wisely; a salutary admonition to set aside this or that fault; financial support, in order to be able to cover the most necessary expenses in many a moment of embarrassment; the favor of a powerful man <note>original: "eines Grossen"; literally "a Great One," referring to a person of high rank or political influence.</note> in order to advance, or to maintain oneself in the position where one currently stands.

A human being certainly needs benevolent friends who cheer him up in hours of discontent <term>Mißvergnügen: a state of being out of sorts, dissatisfied, or in low spirits common in high-pressure social environments</term>; console him over misfortunes suffered, and give him courage when fear takes hold of his heart.

Still others are needed who speak of his merits; who reveal to him the schemes <note>original: "Anschläge"; can also mean plots or strikes against one's reputation.</note> of his enemies; who defend him against them, come to his aid in his undertakings, and thus there are a thousand kinds of services that depend on the benevolence of others.

It is not easily possible for a single person—our friend—to be able to perform all these services; for however much he might perhaps wish to, it is often not within his power. One must therefore make friends of all sorts of people, excluding only the wicked.

What one person cannot achieve, another can; and what the individual is unable to do on their own is nonetheless accomplished through the united assistance <term>Beistand: help or support provided by others, often in a social or political context</term> of several.

To prevent any misunderstanding, I must make the observation here that, in order to make such friends, a perfect alliance of friendship <note>original: "Freundschaftsbündniß"; refers to a formal, deep, or intimate bond of mutual commitment</note> is not required.

Decorum in manners <term>Sitten: the established social customs and moral behaviors of a particular society</term>, polite behavior, the endeavor to make people feel obliged to us, a willingness to serve, and a proactive benevolence will easily win us the affection of the people with whom we associate, so that, when the opportunity arises, one can rely on their gratitude and lay claim to their kindness.

further <note>This "further" connects to the final sentence of the previous page.</note> with a resentful look at their more fortunate fellow humans, who shimmer upon the throne of highest happiness: — how, then, if one goes so far as to insult them? If, through contempt and mistreatment, one makes them feel the full severity of their fate and their lowly position, can one still be surprised when a desire for revenge <note>original: "Rachlust"</note> stirs in their hearts? When a neglected education, the roughness of their social class <term>Stand: the rigid social hierarchy of the 18th century</term>, and a lack of knowledge lead them to the most extravagant means of taking revenge? — Of what is the offended self-love <note>original: "Eigenliebe"; in this context, it refers to one's sense of dignity or ego</note> of man not capable? —

Such people are all the more to be feared because they — perhaps sometimes even against their natural character — must hide their hatred and postpone their revenge, because they do not have the power to avenge the suffered humiliation on the spot. Because of this, their hatred becomes inextinguishable and is constantly nourished; the heart becomes ever more embittered against the offender, and the mind incessantly ponders a certain, cruel means to take its revenge.

One is greatly deceived if one believes oneself so elevated by rank, prestige, and power that their arrows could not reach so far; in vain does one consider oneself safe from their revenge at the highest summit of power and reputation. Hatred and the thirst for revenge <note>original: "Rachlust"</note> are very ingenious <note>The original "sinnreiche" suggests these passions are inventive and clever in finding ways to manifest.</note> passions. The snake that coils beneath your foot will kill you with its sting, while you, reckless one! proudly mock its helplessness.

Time and opportunity will finally provide your enemies with means of which you never thought.

These unfortunate people from the lowest social class <term>Menschenklasse: literally "class of humans," referring to the rigid social stratification of the 18th century</term> are capable of undertaking anything; they dare everything because they have nothing to lose, and however helpless and weak they may always be, it is nevertheless dangerous to incur their hatred.

It is certain; every person can harm me; he only needs a wicked heart to desire it, and cunning <note>original: "Verschlagenheit," implying a crafty or devious intelligence</note> of mind to wait for the right moment and to seize the opportunity.

There are people who seem cold enough to you that they appear to endure insults with the greatest indifference; but from that moment on, they have sworn irreconcilable hatred toward you, and they take revenge on you as often as they can.

One should especially guard against incurring the hatred of the refined, dissimulating <term>dissimulirenden: from the Latin "dissimulare," meaning to hide one's true feelings, character, or intentions</term> courtier; he remains silent; even if he has the power to punish you on the spot for your indiscretion <note>original: "Unbesonnenheit," referring to a lack of reflection or a rash, thoughtless action</note>, he does not do so; he suppresses even the natural surges of his anger, because perhaps this opportunity is not sufficient for him, and he wishes to postpone his revenge to let you feel it more acutely another time.

They belong to that species of **vermin** <note>original: "Gewürme," literally "worms" or "creeping things," used here as a derogatory term for treacherous or lowly individuals</note>, whose anger is easily provoked and whose venom is always fatal. If it is sometimes dangerous to have enemies among those who are beneath us; how much more should one be careful not to incur the hatred of those who are our equals—and who thus have more power to cause harm—or to displease those **above us**, who can ruin us in an instant.

To cause offense is such a simple thing; it is far more difficult to make amends for an insult and to reconcile with the person who has been offended.

## Reconciliation with those with whom one has fallen out.

---

People who stubbornly refuse to reconcile with their enemies show that they have little religion <note>In this 18th-century context, "Religion" refers not just to a specific faith, but to piety and the practice of Christian virtues like forgiveness.</note>, and that their nature approaches that of the wild beast more than the civilized <note>original: "gebildeten," referring to someone who is educated, refined, or cultured</note> human being; they resemble the bear, whose blind rage does not subside until he has torn the object of his anger to pieces.

Hatred does not dwell in a good heart, and even if it does force its way in, it is not powerful enough to rob it of those gentle impulses, that happy readiness, which easily persuade it toward every reasonable <note>original: "billigen," which in this archaic sense means fair, equitable, or just, rather than "inexpensive."</note> settlement.

I freely acknowledge that if someone seeks our life or our honor, we do not so easily forgive our enemies. Yet, let it be so; for however much harder it is for us to overcome our hatred, this victory is an all the more glorious sign of greatness of soul <note>original: "Seelengröße," a term equivalent to the classical concept of magnanimity or a "large-souled" character.</note>.

A nobler spirit, gentler feelings, and a more refined education <note>original: "Bildung," referring to the 18th-century ideal of moral and intellectual cultivation.</note> are required for this; ordinary, everyday people are not capable of such a noble deed.

One finds only a few who have achieved such mastery over their passions that they forget the insults they have suffered and open their arms for brotherly reconciliation.

Do not waste a single moment in making amends for the wrong if you have offended a noble person; let the reconciliation with him be a celebration for you, and restrain yourself from committing new offenses.

## On Duelling.

---

In the barbaric ages <note>original: "barbarischen Zeiten," referring to the historical periods such as the Middle Ages when "trial by combat" was a recognized legal method.</note>, people believed they had to prove their innocence with the sword and wash away insults with blood; and this cruel prejudice <note>original: "Vorurtheil," here used to describe a deep-seated, irrational social custom or bias rather than modern "prejudice" against a specific group.</note> has persisted even into our own times.

Once, people murdered one another legally and with festive pomp—over a single word that was misinterpreted;—over a mere suspicion when they felt their honor <term>Ehre | honor; in this context, it refers to the rigid social code of the upper classes that demanded violent satisfaction for any perceived slight.</term> had been offended:—those barbaric times are over; we live in a century of refinement <note>The author likely refers to the Enlightenment, an era that championed reason and civility over "barbaric" tradition.</note>—and yet this prejudice still lingers.

What nonsense from people who, only a few moments ago, hand

# On the Use of Time.

---

Work alone makes life
bearable for us, and the wise

rest.

make no better use of time

steps <note>original: *heiligen Fußtritten*</note> everywhere.

The lazy **idler** is despised everywhere; he who clings to a sluggish **life of pleasure**, flees all useful and decent business, and seeks only to amuse himself, will not be able to count on any man’s true respect.

Their **inactivity** first made them useless members of **society**; but now they also become a burden to the earth—they become **criminals**, and for the most part, a shameful end to their days awaits them.

## How Should One Fill One’s Idle
## Hours?

---

A distaste for solitude is mostly a certain sign of narrow-mindedness <note>original: *Kleingeistigkeit* | refers to a lack of intellectual depth, petty character, or a limited perspective</note> or of a person's moral corruption.

Yet there are many who cannot be alone for even half an hour without feeling boredom. They do not know how to apply their time and are therefore restless and fretful; solitude makes them sad; they become unbearable to themselves.

A person of sound mind <note>original: *solidem Geiste* | an intellect that is firm, well-cultivated, and reliable</note> knows how to make use of every moment of their life; and such a person is never more usefully employed than when in solitude.

They lead us into the sanctuary <note>original: *Heiligthum*</note> of nature and open for us the richest sources of innocent pleasures. We coax tones from instruments that harmonize with the mood of our soul, or draw the image of our condition in expressive strokes; we make the ideal of our wishes visible and rejoice to see the children of our imagination <note>original: *Einbildungskraft* | referring to the creative faculty of the mind</note> before us; or we describe our pleasure in happy songs—our pain in solemn mourning songs.

Experience shows us the advantages of such a use of our leisure <note>original: *Muße*</note> in the brightest light and assures us that the application of this principle contributes infinitely to our happiness.

# Pride.

---

Why should we be so taken with our own merit <note>original: *Verdienst*</note>, and prefer ourselves to so many others who perhaps have incomparably more value than we do?

Are we made of better material than our fellow human <note>original: *Nebenmensch* | literally "next-person," referring to our neighbors or fellow mankind</note>; are our souls not the breath of one and the same Creator; are they not of the same kind, and does the soul ennoble itself merely according to the scale of conventional advantages?

If advantages that we owe to nature or to chance <note>original: *Zufall* | can also mean coincidence or fortune</note> make us proud, it is a sure sign of a weak mind <note>original: *Geist* | in this context, the intellect or spirit</note>, for in themselves these advantages

## On Sincerity,

---

How? Recommending sincerity in a book on worldly wisdom <note>original: *Weltklugheit*; in the 18th century, this referred to the practical knowledge and savvy required to navigate social circles and political life successfully.</note>? — Is sincerity compatible with politics <note>original: *Politik*; here referring not just to statecraft, but to the calculated maneuvering and social "policy" one uses to manage interpersonal relationships.</note>? —

Most certainly with the true kind! — Can one not be wise and upright <note>original: *rechtschaffen*; implying a person of integrity and moral soundness.</note> at the same time? — and sincerity belongs so essentially to the upright man that he ceases to be an honest man as soon as he becomes insidious, false, and a liar.

This virtue, as essential as it is to the noble person, is so little known in our times, and therefore it seems very useful to me to [tell] my readers some— <note>The sentence is interrupted here by the end of the page; the catchword suggests it continues with "something true" or "truthful."</note>

...to give a true concept of it; for I certainly believe one cannot get to know it without loving it, unless the intellect is entirely occupied by the base principles of a false policy <note>original: *Politik*; here meaning the calculating and often deceptive maneuvering used to gain social or political advantage.</note>, and the heart corrupted by the examples of crawling, snake-like politicians.

When he notices that more is expected of him than he can fulfill, he explains his intentions without reservation, so as not to feed people with vain hope.

Most people have a false concept of sincerity <term>Aufrichtigkeit; the virtue of being open and honest, traditionally seen as a middle ground between being overly secretive and being tactlessly blunt</term>. Many consider it "sincere" when a person, without reflection or modesty, reveals their secrets to everyone and tells blunt truths without the slightest consideration—truths that are bound to cause offense everywhere.

Now they say: is it not obvious that the sincere man is hated everywhere, persecuted, and used as a plaything by the cunning? Consequently, they call the man "court-wise" <note>original: *hofklug*; this term describes the calculating, often deceptive social savvy required to navigate the treacherous environment of a royal court</note> who never speaks the truth and has made it a firm principle of prudence to deceive the world through pretense.

Thus, people always abandon one extreme only to embrace the other.

# Gratitude.

---

**T**he lowest villain cannot help but have respect for the honest man, and admire in him what he himself does not do.

Therefore, the grateful person is esteemed by everyone, the ungrateful themselves not excluded.

Gratitude is a natural duty, and admits no exception.

A good heart feels the full power of this natural law, and it is always proof of a noble, sublime soul when a person has a true feeling for acts of kindness <note>original: "Wohlthaten"; this refers to benefits, favors, or charitable deeds received from others</note>.

The Conduct of the Wise <term>Politik des Weisen; in 18th-century philosophy, "Politik" often referred to "social wisdom" or the practical art of living and interacting with others, rather than government policy</term>.

Know that people value their opinions more than their worldly possessions; read history and count the millions of bloody sacrifices resulting from the diversity of opinions. ## On Proper
## Conduct.

---

Whoever wishes to behave properly and live according to the laws of social propriety <term>Wohlstand: in this historical context, this refers to decorum, decency, and the "well-standing" of a community rather than modern financial wealth</term>, must treat every person according to their station and in a noble manner.

To our superiors we owe reverence; to our teachers: obedience; toward our equals we must behave politely, and toward those who are below us, we must act with benevolence.

We must treat our subordinates with gentleness and kindness if they faithfully fulfill their duty; and if they do not do so, we should direct them to it with seriousness, but never in a harsh or cru— <note>The word "grau=" is the beginning of "grausam" (cruel), which is interrupted by the page break</note>

...cruelly toward them, nor demean yourself through excessive familiarity and intimacy <note>original: "Gemeinschaft" — here referring to social association or closeness that might undermine a superior's authority or standing</note>.

Reprimands and punishments bear no fruit when your own actions show the opposite. It is not enough that you exhort your subordinates to fulfill their duties and punish them if they do not obey you; lead them by your own example, and they will follow you.

How can you rebuke a fault in your neighbor <note>original: "Nächsten" — used here in the broader sense of one's fellow man or those within one's social circle</note>, and punish him for it, when you commit it yourself?

He who leads his neighbor with a good example shows him the safest and easiest path to virtue.

## Concerning the Respect Due to the
### Common Man.

---

This is not so much a principle of prudence <note>original: "Klugheit" — in this context, it refers to strategic social intelligence or "common sense" pragmatism</note> as it is truly a duty.

If the common man shows reverence to the superior in consideration of birth, rank, or dignity, then it is a duty to show the common man the respect he deserves as a human being and as a useful citizen of the state.

It is often only prevailing prejudice that bows the back of the common man before ribbons and stars <note>symbols of aristocratic titles and military orders</note>, or golden garments, while the person who wears these signs of pomp often possesses not the slightest merit.

But the respect shown to the common man is always based on inner worth. His dusty face, his rough <note>original: "schrosigten" — likely an archaic variation of "schrundig" or "schroff," referring to chapped, cracked, or calloused skin</note> hands, his sweat-dripping brow are the medals <note>original: "Ordenszeichen" — literally the insignia of a knightly order, here used metaphorically to contrast peasant labor with aristocratic honors</note> of his merit.

You make him discouraged and distrustful, and you diminish his diligence. Another time, he will subtract from the quality of the work and materials, or from the punctuality of the delivery, exactly what you scrimped from his earnings.

Do not make the earnings you grant him even more difficult through improper or exaggerated criticism, or through unnecessary, merely headstrong alterations; you will gain nothing by it.

Even if the character of the joker <note>original: "Spaßmachers." This refers to someone who habitually seeks to be funny or a "buffoon."</note> and that of the wise man can sometimes be found together, they are nonetheless usually opposites.

## Be Silent and Listen.

---

People want to shine in social circles; everyone wants to stand out above the others; they want to demonstrate the strength of their intellect and the richness of their knowledge <note>original: "Wissenschaften," referring here to general learning and scholarship.</note>; they therefore enjoy speaking, and want only themselves to be heard.

Whoever speaks little and listens to them attentively will certainly please them.

A chatterbox <note>original: "Schwätzer," a derogatory term for someone who talks incessantly without substance.</note> seems to view all his listeners as ignorant, for whom he deigns to have the grace to instruct.

On the other hand, all these big talkers <note>original: "Vielredner"</note> are held to be fools <note>original: "Thoren," an archaic spelling of "Toren," meaning those lacking in wisdom or judgment.</note> who are far too conceited.

# The best of undertakings can come to an unfortunate end.

---

Most of our intentions lie in the hands of fortune <note>original: "Glückes," which in this context refers to external chance or fate rather than personal happiness.</note>; we may have initiated a matter in the best possible way, and yet fortune suddenly shatters our entire edifice.

Fortune may well destroy our intentions, but it can never rob us of the honor of having acted according to the principles of prudence <note>original: "Klugheit," a key Enlightenment virtue referring to the ability to govern oneself by use of reason and foresight.</note>.

### Politics of the Wise Man. R

<image-desc>A small decorative woodcut headpiece ornament featuring stylized symmetrical foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>

It is enough if one is conscious of their own skill <note>original: "Geschicklichkeit," referring here to the practical competence or dexterity of the actor.</note> and cannot reproach themselves for having overlooked anything in their undertakings.

The good or bad success of the matter must neither increase nor diminish the applause that the execution deserves.

Yet the majority of people judge differently: the fortunate or unfortunate outcome is the only thing that determines their judgment, by which they approve of or condemn a person's ruin.

They are unable to break the shell and penetrate into the inner essence of the matter; therefore, they judge everything by the exterior.

## Knowledge that one must have of the spirit of one’s century.

---

People are indeed always the same in their fundamental nature; however, time and circumstances create the distinctions that characterize the modern man as compared to those of previous centuries.

A person who was perhaps the most refined and skillful courtier <term>Hofmann: a member of a royal court, typically one well-versed in etiquette and political maneuvering</term> in the 12th century would be very much out of place <note>original: *verlegen*; suggests being socially awkward, clumsy, or ill-adapted to the current era's customs</note> in our own day.

The court is much like the theater; love and ambition are the usual material <note>original: *Stoff*; literally "fabric" or "thematic material"</note> of the play;

This refinement made hearts sparkle like the most brightly polished steel; but to maintain this high polish, they also had to be hardened, just as steel is.

## Nothing should be neglected.

Useful as this principle <note>original: *Grundsatz*; a fundamental rule or maxim of conduct</note> is in human life, it is nonetheless rarely followed.

## Interaction with Wise and Sensible People.

---

We are born into a deep ignorance of everything that is and that happens around us.

The studies to which our youth is dedicated only begin to break, if even a little, through the thick darknesses that envelop our spirit.

--- Page 333 ---
<meta>This page continues the essay "Interaction with Wise and Sensible People," following the introductory thought that youth only begins to dispel the darkness of ignorance. The catchword "Only" from the previous page is the first word here.</meta>

<header>-><image-desc>A horizontal floral ornament featuring delicate scrolling leaves and blossoms.</image-desc><-</header>

It is only then, through interaction with the wider world, that we acquire the small amount of knowledge that teaches us proper behavior.

However, this limited knowledge is not sufficient for a person who wishes to seek their fortune in the world and become useful to themselves and their fellow citizens.

In our youth, we mostly learn only the basic principles of the sciences <note>The term "Wissenschaften" in this period referred generally to all branches of systematic knowledge and academic study, including the humanities and social sciences, rather than just the natural sciences.</note>, and very little of our professional affairs; how much, then, remains to be made up for later?

Perhaps a person possesses neither the leisure nor the mental strength to learn by themselves everything that is useful or agreeable to them.

In order to educate oneself nonetheless, one can do nothing better than to seek the company of learned scholars and skillful people.

# One must never maintain social contact with frivolous, narrow-minded people.

### Words move; examples lead to action.

Words, when combined with examples, possess such power that it becomes extremely difficult to resist the impression they make upon us:

### Caution and Prudence in Business

---

In the way an affair <term>Geschäft</term> <note>While *Geschäft* means "business" in modern German, here it refers more broadly to any significant undertaking, negotiation, or official duty.</note> is handled and brought to a close, there often depends our own welfare and the well-being of our fellow man—or perhaps even that of an entire state—as well as our honor and our entire future happiness. ## On what one must observe during the most important undertakings.

---

In great undertakings, it often comes down to winning everything or losing everything.

Since these always carry very dangerous consequences if they do not end successfully <note>original: *glücklich*. In the 18th century, this word often meant "fortunate" or "successful" rather than just the emotion of happiness.</note>, one should certainly exercise all possible caution before embarking upon them.

First and foremost, one must never even dare the thought of an important undertaking <term>Unternehmen</term> <note>This refers to any significant venture, whether a business project, a social movement, or a personal mission.</note> unless one knows oneself to be strong enough to tackle it well and bring it to a successful conclusion.

## On Silence.

---

The greatest politicians <note>In the 18th-century context, "politician" often referred broadly to anyone skilled in the "art of worldly wisdom" or statecraft, rather than just elected officials.</note> would labor in vain if they did not keep their intentions secret.

All plans, however well-conceived they may be, must for the most part fail if they are discovered by those whose interest it is to work against them.

The most sound measures <term>Maßregeln</term> <note>While *Maßregeln* can mean "disciplinary actions" today, here it refers to strategic steps or administrative measures taken to achieve a specific goal.</note> are thwarted; through the untimely disclosure of the secret, the opponent anticipates every plan that was devised against him.

Does the scarcity of fidelity <term>Treue</term> <note>In this context, "Treue" refers to both personal loyalty and the reliability one shows in keeping their word.</note> among men not make it a necessary law to investigate and test them with every possible caution before one confides in them? —

When I say that a secret should be inviolable and sacred, I do not yet demand that this should apply universally and entirely without exception. There are cases that not only release me from the duty of maintaining silence <term>Stillschweigen</term> <note>This term implies a deliberate, active state of keeping quiet or being "hushed" about a specific matter.</note>, but even make disclosure <term>Entdeckung</term> <note>In this 18th-century context, "Entdeckung" refers to the act of uncovering or revealing something hidden, rather than a scientific discovery.</note> my duty.

## Hope and Despair.

---

People, who should follow only the light of enlightened reason <note>original: "aufgeklärten Vernunft." In the 18th century, "Reason" was viewed as the ultimate guide for a moral and successful life, meant to override impulsive emotions.</note>, generally judge the nature of things according to their whims and their temperaments <note>According to the "Four Humors" theory prevalent at the time, a person's "temperament" (sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric, or melancholic) determined their outlook on life.</note>.

The person who is full of himself, always accustomed to flattering his own ego, does not doubt in the least that he will receive everything he desires.

The fearful man, on the other hand, who trusts neither himself nor others, almost always despairs of the successful outcome of his undertakings.

Carefully avoid these dangerous extremes; too little and too much—

<margin>The Conduct of the Wise Man.</margin>
<u>u</u>

**Vocabulary:** <term>Hope</term>, <term>Despair</term>, <term>Reason</term>, <term>Temperaments</term>, <term>The Conduct of the Wise</term>, <term>Extremes</term>

<summary>The author warns that human judgment is often clouded by personal temperament rather than reason, leading people toward either blind overconfidence or paralyzing fear. He advocates for a middle path, which he calls the "Conduct of the Wise Man."</summary>
<keywords>hope, despair, reason, temperament, overconfidence, fear, Enlightenment philosophy, emotional balance</keywords>

## Indecision.

---

People who have no definite purpose, and are always indecisive <note>original: "unschlüßig"</note> about what they ought to do, wander through the world almost as aimlessly as a traveler in a gloomy forest where he does not know the paths.

One must endeavor to become acquainted with the various classes <term>Stände: historically referring to the "estates" or social orders, such as the clergy, nobility, and commoners, which defined one's role in the world</term> of civil society in good time, and then embrace that one which is most suited to a person's talents and strengths.

## Precipitancy in Judgment.

One must also never be over-hasty in one's judgment. Blinded by error and prejudices <note>The author uses "prejudices" (Vorurtheilen) in the Enlightenment sense—meaning preconceived notions or biases that cloud one's ability to see objective truth.</note>, one will never find the truth.

Whence come so many errors of all kinds? — Whence so many false principles <term>Grundsätze: fundamental rules or maxims that guide a person's conduct</term>, according to which a multitude of people act, and are made unhappy? —

It arises from this: that people do not wish to give themselves the trouble to seek the truth in things through simple reflection <note>Original: "Nachdenken," implying deep, careful thought</note>, and to investigate from which side a matter may best be carried out.

Correctness and the truth of things do not present themselves to the mind immediately—

## On the Manner in Which One Should Deal with Those Who Have Served Us in Any Business.

# On the External Appearance of Man.

---

The principle of some false politicians <note>In the 18th and early 19th centuries, "politician" (Politiker) often referred to worldly schemers or people who used social manipulation to get ahead, rather than just government officials</note>: **One must seem to be everything, and be nothing**, is the lowest and most ruinous that false politics has ever devised.

This principle, if it could ever become universal, would turn human beings into the most contemptible creatures; it would rob them of everything that creates their happiness, secures their well-being, and determines their worth.

### On the passions that still dominate the elderly.

---

Every person will find much more favor in the world the more they conduct themselves in accordance with their social standing and their age.

In a monarch, we are pleased by a grand, majestic air; in judges and persons of authority, we expect a solemn brow; a proud, fiery gaze heightens the prestige of a hero, and we admire it in the commander of an army.

Just so, one likes to see a cheerful, lively disposition in a youth, and gravity <note>original: "Ernst," implying a serious, dignified, and sober demeanor</note> in an old man.

<vocab>Passions, Monarch, Judge, Heroes, Commander, Army, Youth, Elderly man</vocab>

It contrasts the appropriate traits for different roles, such as the majesty of a king, the solemnity of a judge, and the gravity of the elderly.</summary>
<keywords>decorum, social status, aging, passions, authority, professional conduct, etiquette, maturity</keywords>

## The wicked person must never hope for support from us.

---

Nothing is more beautiful, and testifies more to a noble heart <note>original: "edeln Herzen" — referring to a person of high moral character and generosity.</note>, than doing good to all people, not even excepting our greatest enemies; — but the wicked <note>original: "der Böse" — this refers to a person who acts immorally or maliciously.</note> must not be able to promise himself any support <note>original: "Unterstützung" — in this context, it implies aiding or endorsing his harmful character or projects.</note> from us.

I do not mean by this that one should hate him, or perhaps think that one does not even owe him what he can demand of us as a human being:

The wicked man — even if he were the greatest villain — remains always a human being, and as a human being in need, in misfortune, in sickness, in danger of death, and in death, he is worthy <note>The catchword "werth" from the metadata completes the grammatical sense here: "worthy of our compassion."</note> of our compassion and our help.

<vocab>Wicked/Evil, Support, Noble heart, Enemies, Human being, Compassion, Help</vocab>

<summary>This page distinguishes between providing humanitarian aid to a "wicked" person in distress and offering support for their character or deeds. It argues that while one should never aid a person's malice, their status as a human being entitles them to basic compassion and help in times of suffering.</summary>
<keywords>ethics, morality, humanity, compassion, wicked, support, enemies, noble heart</keywords>

worthy <note>This continues the thought from the previous page: "...the wicked man... is worthy of our compassion and our help."</note>, and I do not believe that there can be such a degenerate <note>original: "verarteten" — meaning someone who has strayed from their better nature or become debased.</note> human being who would not be moved by kind treatment in a time of need, such that he receives a sense of what is good and learns to see the abhorrence of his own actions.

## One Must Defend the Rights of Virtue.

---

It is always a duty to quietly inform those who hold power of the villainous deeds <term>Bubenstücken: literally "boyish tricks," but used here to mean malicious, underhanded, or villainous acts</term> with which people seek to suppress innocence; or even to be a public defender oneself if one is in a position to save them; one must rush to help and courageously begin the battle against the base oppressor, whatever may come of it.

[appoint]ments <note>Completing the word "Bedienstungen" from the previous page.</note> only according to favor, or surrender them for money, they are the greatest disaster for the land they govern.

By thus auctioning off positions to the highest bidder, they commit the most inexcusable injustice against the state; for the proverb—**He who buys an office, in turn sells justice**—proves true, unfortunately, all too often.

These office-buyers <note>original: "Dienstkäufer"; this refers to the historical practice of "venality of office," where administrative or judicial posts were sold as private property.</note> usually profiteer with justice, bleed the subject <note>original: "Unterthan"; a person living under the rule of a sovereign.</note> dry, and bargain away the welfare of the Prince and the country as often as they can. The sum they paid for the position is soon recouped through extortion, fraud, and breach of trust; but that is the least of it; many make it their aim to amass treasures not for themselves alone, but for their entire family, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and a whole generation.

<term>Injustice (Unrecht): A violation of the rights of others or the law.</term>
<term>Proverb (Sprichwort): A traditional saying expressing a perceived truth.</term>

## Feelings that interaction with our
## fellow creatures, and their use,
## should instill in us.

---

Can many of the creatures of this earth, which seem to exist for our ruin <note>original: "Verderben"; referring to creatures that seem harmful or destructive to humans.</note>, or are truly harmful to us, not also contribute to our well-being?

If we know how to make good use of them, and cherish such feelings for them as are worthy of a good human heart, then the goodness and loveliness they possess will also command us to love the One <note>A reference to the Creator.</note> who gave them existence <note>original: "Daseyn"</note> and everything they are; and their imperfection, their evil, will ensure that we feel no undue attachment <unclear>toward</unclear> <note>original: "Neigu[ng]"; meaning a leaning or misplaced devotion to worldly things over spiritual ones.</note> them.

<vocab>**Fellow creatures**, **Well-being**, **Human heart**, **Existence**, **Imperfection**</vocab>

<summary>This page introduces a moral philosophy regarding the natural world, arguing that even harmful or "imperfect" animals serve a spiritual purpose by directing human love toward the Creator rather than the creatures themselves. It marks a transition from social etiquette to the ethics of man's relationship with nature.</summary>
<keywords>natural theology, ethics, fellow creatures, creation, well-being, imperfection, human heart</keywords>

--- Page 439 ---
<meta>This page continues the theological and ethical reflection begun on page 374, moving from the observation of animals to the contemplation of human nature and the universe as a whole. It continues the argument that earthly beauty and virtue are reflections of the divine.</meta>

375

The beauty of the entire universe, and especially that of rational beings <note>original: "vernünftigen Wesen"; referring to humans as beings capable of reason.</note>, will give us a concept of the supreme beauty of the Creator, and awaken in us the desire to be united with him forever.

Reason <note>original: "Verstand"; often translated as intellect or understanding in this philosophical context.</note>, strength, goodness, wisdom, fairness, and other qualities valued in humans, lead us to the admiration of divine perfections, which are the source of all our virtues and the foundation of all our life's blessings.

The joys enjoyed here below <note>original: "hienteden"; an archaic German term for life on earth as opposed to the afterlife.</note>, which one pursues with such great desire—however much they may sometimes be embittered by misfortunes—can teach us to reflect on how great those must be that await us in a better world, and they become an ever stronger impulse to perfect ourselves for the future.

# The Politics of the Wise.

## On Politeness, and What is Called Propriety <term>Wohlstand|In this historical context, 'Wohlstand' refers not to financial wealth, but to 'decorum' or 'propriety'—the state of behaving in a way that is fitting for one’s social position.</term>.

Politeness is one of the most important du-
ties of a person in soci-
ety, and belongs just as preeminently
to worldly wisdom <term>Lebensklugheit|The art of living or practical wisdom; the ability to navigate social and personal affairs with prudence and tact.</term>.

One can be virtuous without
being polite; but one will certainly not 
make oneself likable without 
politeness.

Indeed, by making virtue itself 
contemptible and hateful through 
a lack of politeness, one often 
exposes oneself to the greatest humiliations.

<image-desc>A small decorative horizontal ornament consisting of stylized foliage and a central floral motif.</image-desc>

Impoliteness <note>original: "Unhöflichkeit"</note> is generally displeasing, and reveals a thoughtless person who is only occupied with themselves, and focuses their attention on nothing but themselves.

Rudeness <note>original: "Grobheit"</note> offends—often to the point of being unforgivable—and always proves that the person has made it a habit to neglect themselves, or is constantly in bad company.

A crude, vulgar behavior <note>The original word "pöbelhaftes" refers to the "Pöbel" or common rabble; in this period, behaving like the lower classes was seen as a significant moral and social failure for a person of standing.</note> causes outrage, and brings all missteps, all the flaws of a poor upbringing <term>Erziehung|Refers to the total moral, social, and academic cultivation of a person, typically managed by parents or tutors.</term>, and often also of a poor conduct, into the clearest light.

Many faults, many weaknesses and vulnerabilities of a person become less visible when they know how to make themselves agreeable through politeness; but nothing is missing, other than also being rude, to reveal everything all at once, and to make oneself hated by everyone.

### 400

To praise qualities in a sensible woman <term>Frauenzimmer|While 'Frauenzimmer' is often used pejoratively in modern German today, in the 18th century it was a neutral, even respectful, term for a woman or lady of status.</term> that she does not possess is an act of mockery; it is hardly different from being openly rude.

Convention <term>Convention|Established social customs and norms of behavior.</term> imposes laws upon us in social life. Even if these laws are not the most rational or the most just <note>original: "die billigsten"; in this context, 'billig' refers to equity and fairness rather than monetary cost.</note>—and are often contrary to our entire way of thinking <term>Denkart|A person’s habitual mindset or moral character.</term>—they must nonetheless be followed if one does not wish to cause offense at every turn, to insult through defiance, or to become ridiculous through eccentricity <term>Singularität|From the Latin 'singularitas'; refers here to a peculiar behavior or a refusal to follow social norms that makes one stand out unfavorably.</term>.

Among these laws are the compulsion to pay compliments <term>Complimenten-Zwang|The social pressure or perceived obligation to offer polite, often hollow, praise in formal settings.</term> and the rules of ceremony <term>Ceremoniel|The formal procedures and etiquette governing social or courtly interactions.</term>.

To the wise man, these things are trivialities; he does not regard them for his own sake; but he will nonetheless not disregard them out of consideration for the people with whom he associates.

One should therefore observe, in titles <term>Titulatūren|Formal modes of address and honorifics used to signify rank and social standing.</term> and ceremony <term>Ceremoniel|The established code of etiquette and protocol required in social or official interactions.</term>, everything that general custom has established; and one should make it a general rule to show everyone not just exactly as much honor <term>Ehre|Social honor or the public recognition of one's worth.</term> as is due to their rank <term>Stand|A person's social status, class, or station in life.</term> and their merits <term>Verdienste|Individual accomplishments or virtues deserving of recognition.</term>, but always a little bit more. For one can safely count on the fact that the conceptions everyone has of their own person, their merits, and their rank tend to exceed the true relationship <term>Verhältniß|One’s actual objective standing or proportion relative to other people.</term> in which they stand with others by several degrees. Thus, one would certainly cause offense if one were to grant only the strictly appropriate measure of respect or reverence <term>Ehrerbietung|The outward manifestation of high regard or deference.</term> and were not willing to bestow a small extra measure besides.

Therefore, we must seek to possess them and bring them to light—if not for his sake, then for their own sake and for our own.

## Miscellaneous Principles and Thoughts on Politeness.

---

Philanthropy <note>The original German *Menschenfreundlichkeit* literally means "friendliness toward people," reflecting the Enlightenment ideal of benevolence and general love for humanity.</note> and politeness have this in common: they both contribute to the welfare of society.

The former bids us to act toward our fellow man with goodness and honesty; the latter bids us to join the goodness of the heart with a pleasant outward appearance, thereby binding him more closely to us.

## Flattery

---

Despise that glinting pseudo-politeness—that pomp of convention which is demanded, and with which one is satisfied, yet which fundamentally matters to no one. It is false politeness, the mask of social decorum <note>original: *Wohlstand*. In 18th-century German, this term often referred to "propriety" or "good breeding" rather than financial wealth.</note>.

Flattery is more than tasteless when it is applied to a person who thinks and who possesses a sensitive soul.

Flattery can only please the mediocre, the common man, and often even the wicked, whom pride has blinded.

## Interaction with the Fair Sex.

---

Everything that one can call a well-mannered, refined man of the world <term>Weltmann</term>; the pleasantness of his social company; the gentle cultivation of his character; the careful enhancement of his outward appearance; a refined taste—a young man certainly acquires all of this through interaction with the fair sex <term>schönen Geschlechte</term> <note>original: *schönen Geschlechte*. A common 18th-century idiom referring to women, emphasizing the perceived civilizing and softening influence they had on male society.</note>.

## Of Credit <term>Kredit</term>.
---

Once someone has lost their credit <note>In this context, "credit" refers to one's social standing, reputation, and the trust others place in them.</note> in the world, it becomes extremely difficult for them to rise up again, or perhaps they never succeed in doing so at all.

I use this word in its broadest sense; not in the more restricted meaning where credit <term>Kredit</term> is only taken to mean the confidence <term>Zutrauen</term> in repayment. By this, I understand everything: confidence in capability and effectiveness <term>Wirkungskraft</term>, in integrity <term>Rechtschaffenheit</term> and honor <term>Ehre</term>, in order, precision, and in the endeavor to work for the welfare of the whole <term>Wohl des Ganzen</term> and the individual to the best of one's abilities.

Therefore, credit is such an indispensable necessity for a person, without

<meta>catchword: which [dem]</meta>

<summary>The author defines 'Credit' as a comprehensive measure of a person's character, encompassing their reputation for honesty, capability, and social responsibility rather than just financial reliability. He argues that once this social trust is lost, it is nearly impossible to recover.</summary>

<keywords>credit, reputation, social trust, integrity, honor, social standing, Enlightenment ethics</keywords>

<page-num>446</page-num>

which he cannot survive in social life <term>gesellschaftlichen Leben</term>, just as necessary as the sustenance required for his very existence.

Therefore, the first thing that one should strive to acquire in the world is credit <note>reputation and social trust</note>.

If you wish for the state <term>Staat</term> to entrust its affairs to you, then give early proof of your insights and your talents; ensure that nothing can be found to criticize in your way of life and conduct; demonstrate integrity <term>Rechtschaffenheit</term>, order, and domesticity <term>Häuslichkeit</term> everywhere. <note>In this era, "domesticity" implied a well-ordered private life, which was seen as a prerequisite for managing public affairs.</note>

Above all, guard yourself so that no one may place mistrust in you regarding these three most essential qualities of a man of business <term>Geschäftsmannes</term>.

A disorderly, profligate life brings even the finest mind, possessed of the most magnificent talents and a good heart, into general discredit <term>Mißkredit</term>.

To acquire credit <note>In this context, "credit" refers to social trust, reputation, and the "capital" of one's good name.</note> in the world, it mostly depends on how one first appears.

If one has completely lost a hard-won reputation <note>original: "Kredit"; here referring to social trust and standing.</note> through an unfortunate action, a bad deed, or through negligence, then one might as well withdraw immediately and should not dare to step forward again.

To maintain this credit <note>original: "Kredit"; in this context, it refers to both a person's financial trustworthiness and their general social reputation.</note>, one must possess good conduct <term>Aufführung</term> <note>While this can mean a theatrical "performance," here it refers to one's behavior and moral presentation in public.</note>, moderate and modest spending, cleanliness and decency in dress, and above all, punctuality in payment.

Therefore, see to it that your payment arrives at the appointed time, and you will always be held in high regard.

There are obstacles that often make punctuality of payment impossible even for the most honest and orderly man—if he relied too gullibly on the word of others, or if he acted too unconcerned by believing he could safely count on the sources he usually drew from, and thus allows the payment deadline to approach. However, these obstacles do not excuse him in the eyes of his creditor <term>Gläubiger</term>, and he will always be looked upon as a man of poor character <note>original: "schlechten Mann"; literally "bad man," implying a lack of reliability or integrity.</note>.

# The Court.

---

The court is the sphere of action for the most refined politics <note>In the 18th century, "politics" (Politik) referred not just to government business, but to the art of social maneuvering, shrewdness, and "policy" in interpersonal relationships.</note>; one must have achieved the greatest possible skill within it in order to survive as an honest man, and to secure oneself against the false politics of many a low-minded, intrigue-obsessed courtier.

Sad is the lot of the noble soul whose fate decrees they live at court, if his heart—entirely without guile and without fruit <note>original: "ohne Frucht." This may be a period-specific idiom for "without result/protection," or a potential printer's error for "Furcht" (fear).</note>—is not covered by the shield of true prudence; if, being unfamiliar with the workings of intrigues and cabals <term>Cabals: Secret plots or small groups of people joined together to overturn those in power through political maneuvering.</term>, he does not know how to make use of politics in order to protect himself against cunning and deception.

Soon he will become the plaything of the lowest schemes, which, for his downfall, are

<summary>This page introduces the court as a treacherous environment where an honest person must master "politics" and prudence to defend themselves against the intrigues of courtiers. It warns that without such skills, a noble-hearted person will inevitably fall victim to the schemes of others.</summary>

devised. As often as honesty, usefulness, and the well-being of the Prince and the State—which demand his services—elevate him once more, just as often does the cabal <note>A cabal refers to a secret political clique or faction involved in intrigue.</note> cast him down again, either in the middle of his undertakings or immediately after successfully rendered services, until he finally sinks completely and is trampled into the dust.

The wise of all ages have never spoken highly of the court, and have warned man against it, sometimes with symbolic imagery and sometimes with clear words; a proof of how dangerous it is to live there, and how detrimental it often is to a person's happiness—and even to the goodness of their moral character.

Pride, self-interest, and a tendency toward debauchery <note>original: "Wohllust." In the 18th century, this term suggested a broader sense of sensual indulgence, luxury, and physical pleasure rather than just modern "lust."</note>—man's most dangerous passions—find ample nourishment at courts and, unless one is exceptionally vigilant, grow into terrible, heaven-storming giants.

## At Court
### one must be distrustful.

---

Who, after everything previously established, does not see that carefree **confidence** <term>Zutrauen</term> and the **openness** of a free, guileless heart are among the most dangerous errors at court; and that for one's own **self-preservation** <term>Selbsterhaltung</term>, one must necessarily trust no one?
