I have said that one must be reserved toward every person whom one does not yet know well enough;—now consider: at **court** <term>Hof</term> you are always among strangers, people unknown to you, for you will perhaps never come to know them completely throughout your entire life.

One must view the court as a **hostile land**, where a thousand **snares** <note>The author uses the word "Fallstricke," literally pitfalls or tripwires used in hunting, to describe social traps.</note> are set to outwit us.

There at court, people possess the most **decorum** <term>Anstand</term> <note>In this context, "Anstand" refers to the polished outward display of manners and etiquette required by high society.</note> but the least **sincerity** <term>Aufrichtigkeit</term>.

Do not trust their artificial **flatteries**, their false **familiarity**; reflect that their generally accepted principle is to appear outwardly as something entirely different from what they are within.

This man smiles at you kindly and shows you his **favor** <term>Gewogenheit</term>, yet seeks only an opportunity to destroy you.

# On the Great.

---

What is a **Great One** <term>Grosser</term>? <note>In this context, "the Great" refers to the high nobility, aristocrats, and powerful ministers who populated the royal courts.</note> — Is it a rational, instructed, modest, sensitive, and virtuous human being? Is it at least a person who follows **natural law** <note>The concept that certain rights or values are inherent by virtue of human nature and can be understood through reason.</note>, and possesses some good qualities? —

You will find no one who is everything that is asked here; and no one who is the opposite of it all.

See in the Great at **court** <term>Hofe</term> neither gods, nor those **cast out of hell** <term>Verworfre der Hölle</term> — see them as humans, who have their passions, weaknesses, virtues, and vices, and who on the **danger-**

How much is a great man <note>The "Great" (*ein Großer*) refers to a member of the high nobility or a person of high social rank.</note> in this situation to be pitied! — Everything lays snares for his heart; everything prepares dangers for him.

The first thing a person of rank usually knows, when he begins to think and feel, is that he is great, rich, and will one day be powerful; yet is that not precisely the last thing he should know? — He knows already so early that there are poor, unfortunate people who will crawl like despised worms beneath his feet, and learns too late, or often not at all, that these too are human beings, his fellow brothers; that he has no advantage over these worms except for fortune <note>original: *Glück*. Referring to the high-ranking nobility.</note> is to strike fear into the **common man**; but how quickly would this fear vanish if one were to consider for once that the great and the small stand under one and the same **sovereign**, that great and small are governed by the very same **laws**, and that these laws are rarely without effect if one summons them with **courage** for one's defense.

This courage, however, is something quite unusual among so many who are weak and fearful; it requires more heart to destroy a **power of the imagination** than to offer brave resistance to **actual force**. <note>The author suggests that the "greatness" of the nobility is a psychological spell or social illusion ("Einbildung") that is harder to break than fighting physical violence ("Gewalt").</note>

6.) Show true gratitude for the favors <note>original: *Gnaden*; literally "graces," referring to the specific kindnesses or privileges granted by a superior</note> you receive, and prove, by doubling your zeal for the service of your master or your benefactor, how deeply you feel the greatness of your good fortune.

Act according to these principles in the use of courtly favor, and in doing so, you will compel the Great <note>original: *die Großen*; refers to high-ranking nobility or those in positions of power</note> to never withdraw their goodwill from you.
